black.label: Black history
black.description: Challenges racist historical narratives and recovers Black agency, institutions, and political struggle. Abolitionism, community scholarship, and Black institutions provide independent roots, not merely applications of European theory.
black.representative_figures_and_works: William Wells Brown; George Washington Williams (1882–83); Carter G. Woodson; W. E. B. Du Bois, Black Reconstruction (1935). Carter G. Woodson and colleagues founded the Association for the Study of Negro Life and History (now ASALH) in 1915. Postwar and later examples include John Hope Franklin, From Slavery to Freedom (1947), and Darlene Clark Hine, Black Women in White (1989).

women.label: Women’s history
women.date_label: Nineteenth-century and interwar work; renewed expansion from the 1960s
women.description: Studies women as historical actors and examines work, family, politics, and structures of power. Earlier scholarship, activism, teaching, and documentary collecting precede the field’s expansion alongside later feminist movements. Recovery, institutional growth, rediscovery, and methodological disagreement overlap; this is not a field created from nothing in the 1960s or one account of a shared female experience.
women.representative_figures_and_works: Lucy Maynard Salmon, Domestic Service (1897); Alice Clark (1919); Ivy Pinchbeck (1930); Julia Cherry Spruill (1938); Mary Ritter Beard (1946); Eleanor Flexner (1959); Eileen Power; Dorothy Thompson; later work by Gerda Lerner and Sheila Rowbotham. Individual entries distinguish contributions and approaches. Leonore Davidoff and Catherine Hall: Family Fortunes (1987); Elizabeth Fox-Genovese: Within the Plantation Household (1988).

representative_people.context: Investigates domestic employment through both employers and workers, historical change and statistical comparison; she distinguishes inquiry from a cure for household difficulties.
representative_people.works: Domestic Service (1897; expanded second edition 1901); Progress in the Household (1906), Apologia

representative_people.context: Counts paid and unpaid production while distinguishing household forms, class and marital position. Her account of capitalist change retains maternalist assumptions and contested medieval comparisons.
representative_people.works: Working Life of Women in the Seventeenth Century (1919), preface, introduction and conclusion

representative_people.context: Explains changes in women’s work and wages through training, household organization and industrial/agrarian change. Her qualified optimistic interpretation differs from Clark’s longer decline account.
representative_people.works: Women Workers and the Industrial Revolution, 1750–1850 (1930); reprint preface (1969, signed 1968)

representative_people.context: Documents everyday institutions, work and public activity in the colonial South. Richter values its status distinctions but questions its limited inquiry into Black and Native women.
representative_people.works: Women’s Life and Work in the Southern Colonies (1938; Scott introductions for 1972 and 1998 reissues)

representative_people.context: Argues for women’s historical agency while promoting records, catalogues and teaching; her general category of women and institutional practice require critical assessment.
representative_people.works: Woman as Force in History (1946), preface; WCWA work (1935–1940) and collaboration with the Smith collection from the 1940s

women.scope_note: Earlier documentary, economic and institutional projects overlap with later feminist reconstruction and theory. Periodization, class, race, caste and regional contexts create disagreements within women’s history. Gender history develops some of these questions without superseding the field; this roster remains selective and uneven geographically.

strands.title: Earlier histories of work and their disagreements
strands.focus: Clark’s overlapping household forms and Pinchbeck’s industrial transition ask different period questions. Paid and unpaid production, training, marital status and class complicate a single progress/decline story; maternalist commitments remain visible.

strands.title: Documents, rights and historical agency
strands.focus: Beard’s documentary project, Spruill’s colonial study and Flexner’s rights history offer different forms of recovery.
strands.works: Woman as Force in History (1946); Women’s Life and Work (1938); Century of Struggle (1959)

strands.title: Socialist and feminist historical work
strands.focus: Class, community and women’s organizing are connected questions, with differences among practitioners.
strands.works: Outsiders (1993); Hidden from History (1973); Eve and the New Jerusalem (1983)

strands.title: Work and family change
strands.focus: Tilly and Scott question assumptions that women at home were unproductive and that wage work automatically meant emancipation.
strands.works: 1975 joint article; Women, Work, and Family (1978)

strands.title: Period boundaries and historical explanation
strands.focus: Kelly’s Renaissance question and Lerner’s historical account of patriarchy challenge supposedly timeless or universally progressive narratives.
strands.works: “Did Women Have a Renaissance?” (1977); The Creation of Patriarchy (1986)

strands.title: Black women’s historical questions
strands.focus: Slavery, professional institutions, religion and racial analysis are distinct subjects and methods.
strands.works: Black Women in White (1989); Ar’n’t I a Woman? (1985); Righteous Discontent (1993)

strands.title: National and regional syntheses
strands.focus: French collaborative synthesis, German social history and Nigerian women’s history have different scopes and documentary bases.
strands.works: Histoire des femmes, vol. 4 (1991); Women in German History (1989 English); Nigerian Women (1992)

strands.title: Life histories and written lives
strands.focus: Davis, Bozzoli/Nkotsoe and Kaplan use different personal evidence; no single life stands for all women.
strands.works: Women on the Margins (1995); Women of Phokeng (1991); Between Dignity and Despair (1998)

strands.title: Caste and historical patriarchy
strands.focus: Chakravarti examines upper-caste sexual control and social hierarchy through early Indian texts. Prescriptions must be distinguished from lived practices.

strands.title: Medieval women, rules and recorded practice
strands.focus: Power examines the production and survival of visitation evidence and warns against equating a catalogue of faults with the whole life of a community. Her confidence in truthful findings remains an argument to test.

strands.title: Collecting records, access and unequal authority
strands.focus: Preserving documents, making them discoverable and bringing them into teaching involve collective labor. WCWA’s broadened mission and Black women’s limited authority/funding complicate an uncomplicated recovery narrative.
strands.works: WCWA and Smith collecting; Voss-Hubbard (1995); Cott, ed., A Woman Making History (1991)

strands.title: Southern women: documentary scope and later reissues
strands.focus: Spruill distinguishes domestic institutions, public activity and status. Scott’s reissues renew access; Richter values the book while questioning its limited inquiry into Black and Native women.
strands.works: Women’s Life and Work (1938; reissues 1972, 1998); Richter review (1999)

strands.title: Rights movements, archival reach and historical boundaries
strands.focus: Flexner’s labor and Black women’s coverage broadens a suffrage narrative. Rupp distinguishes participants’ self-definition from historians’ expanded categories; James asks a different question about structural explanation.
strands.works: Century of Struggle (1959); James (1960) and Rupp (1992) reception

strands.title: Early modern women, the sexes and the history curriculum
strands.focus: Teaching and essays put women, and the relations between the sexes, into early modern European history. Davis calls the 1971 course the first in women’s history in Canada and Hesse a first in the curriculum; neither is a field origin.
strands.works: Society and the Sexes (course, 1971); “City Women and Religious Change” and “Women on Top” (in Society and Culture, 1975)

global.description: Moves across national containers through comparison, interaction, circulation, and connections. These approaches differ; global scale need not imply one theory of globalization.

strands.focus: Duara frames national, local and transnational histories as potentially conflicting rather than one evolutionary story.

strands.title: Comparison and connection in dispute
strands.focus: Lieberman’s state comparisons and Subrahmanyam’s circulation are interlocutory projects, not successive universal methods.

strands.title: Reciprocal comparison and connected units
strands.focus: Pomeranz names Wong’s reciprocal comparison and Tilly’s encompassing comparison as resources. Regions, states and wider systems answer different questions; the method does not require treating Europe and China as internally uniform.

strands.title: Proto-industry and the limits of trade
strands.focus: Pomeranz extends Mokyr’s labor model across regions while questioning unlimited manufacture exports and resource imports at unchanged relative prices. Comparing regions also requires examining their trading partners.

strands.title: Legal ordering across empires
strands.focus: Benton uses jurisdictional conflicts to ask how local cultural practices formed repeated institutional patterns across empires. This strategy places legal ordering alongside other ways of relating local encounters to global structures. Her 2002 introduction is read; the 2013 volume with Richard J. Ross and Stern’s separate 2011 corporate-sovereignty book are bibliographic resources, not evidence of a single school or transmission.
strands.works: Benton, Law and Colonial Cultures (2002 imprint); Benton and Ross, eds., Legal Pluralism and Empires (2013, body unread). Further comparative resource: Philip J. Stern, The Company-State (2011, publisher metadata only).

strands.title: Capitalism as connected regional diversity
strands.focus: In his 2020 methodological answer Beckert relates regional differences and connections: merchants, plantations, manufacturing and state power belong in the same global inquiry. His account resists treating Europe’s industrialisation as the whole history of capitalism. This strand records his stated strategy; the empirical adequacy of its global applications and criticism of the cotton argument remain open.
strands.works: GrowthPolicy interview with Devjani Roy (2020), answer 2; Empire of Cotton (2014, existing limited excerpt)

historicalsociology.label: Comparative historical sociology
historicalsociology.description: Compares how states, rights, class relations and collective struggles change. Moore studies agrarian routes; Skocpol combines state breakdown with class and international relations; Tilly follows contention; Mann maps intersecting power networks. Bendix, Goldstone, Somers and Block supply different questions about authority, demography, citizenship and economic institutions. Sewell’s exchange with Skocpol makes ideology an explicit debate.
historicalsociology.representative_figures_and_works: Barrington Moore, Social Origins of Dictatorship and Democracy (1966); Theda Skocpol, States and Social Revolutions (1979); Charles Tilly; Michael Mann, The Sources of Social Power I (1986); Perry Anderson (1974).

strands.title: Reconsidering Polanyi
strands.focus: A specific collaborative engagement with economic institutions broadens the field’s conceptual resources.

strands.title: Population, institutions and state crises
strands.focus: Demographic pressures acquire political effects through institutions and elite relations, not population alone.

strands.title: Ideology within structural explanation
strands.focus: Sewell criticizes a restricted account of ideology; Skocpol acknowledges a problem and responds. Her reply’s opening also questions Sewell’s anonymous conception of culture; the exchange contains disagreement in both directions.

strands.title: Interdependence and group power
strands.focus: Court settings and community exclusion are distinct research scales.
strands.works: The Court Society (1969); The Established and the Outsiders (1965)

strands.title: Sport and regulated excitement
strands.focus: Sport opens a further historical problem of affect and interdependence.

strands.title: Comparing crises and their different outcomes
strands.focus: Goldstone compares England and the Fronde, then distinguishes Castile from the Spanish monarchy’s rebellious peripheries. Similar pressures need not produce identical outcomes. Perry values the comparison but questions how far its claims travel across different societies and periods.

strands.title: Empire formation and conflicting political aims
strands.focus: Eisenstadt’s prefaces distinguish social conditions from the emergence of leaders able to organize an imperial polity. Rulers seek resources less bound to traditional groups while trying to control those resources themselves. This comparison retains structural-functional and evolutionary assumptions that his retrospective introduction discusses rather than simply disowns.
strands.works: The Political Systems of Empires (1963), selected prefaces

strands.title: Questioning the units of comparison
strands.focus: Eisenstadt takes up Rokkan’s attention to cultural and territorial settings and questions exporting European state categories. Subrahmanyam separately uses Eurasian circulation to challenge autonomous-state and ideological partitions. These are distinct arguments, not a demonstrated intellectual lineage between the authors.
strands.works: Eisenstadt, Stein Rokkan Lecture (1985); Subrahmanyam, Connected Histories (1997)

strands.title: State legibility and the limits of imposed plans
strands.focus: Scott asks how names, addresses, surveys and standards make societies open to administrative intervention, and how planning is altered by the social practices it encounters. His 2008 account also applies standardization to capitalist firms. These are comparative questions with attributed examples, not a single theory of every state.
strands.works: Seeing Like a State (1998); “Seeing Like a Society,” author interview (2008)

intellectualhistory.label: Intellectual history
intellectualhistory.date_label: Earlier histories of thought · Lovejoy 1936 · Skinner 1969 · plural programmes through the 1990s
intellectualhistory.description: Studies thought, concepts, arguments and their production, circulation and interpretation in historical settings. History of ideas, contextual political thought, conceptual history, textual criticism and the material history of publishing supply overlapping but disputed methods. Intellectual history extends beyond the Cambridge School and beyond a canon of European philosophers.
intellectualhistory.representative_figures_and_works: Arthur O. Lovejoy: The Great Chain of Being (1936); Quentin Skinner: “Meaning and Understanding in the History of Ideas” (1969); J. G. A. Pocock: “The history of political thought” (1962); The Machiavellian Moment (1975); Annabel S. Brett: Liberty, Right and Nature (1997); Reinhart Koselleck: Futures Past (German 1979; English 1985); Dominick LaCapra: Rethinking Intellectual History (1983); John E. Toews: “Intellectual History after the Linguistic Turn” (1987); Robert Darnton: The Business of Enlightenment (1979); Masao Maruyama: Studies in the Intellectual History of Tokugawa Japan (essays 1940–1944; English 1974); Mikiso Hane: English translation of Maruyama’s Studies (1974).

intellectualhistory.scope_note: An enduring field with internal disagreements, not a single lineage from Lovejoy to contextualism. The existing Cambridge School and Conceptual history entries retain their specificity. Maruyama supplies one Japanese inquiry with explicit translation credit, not global representation or evidence of Cambridge influence. Social and cultural settings matter without reducing texts to reflections of social position. Women’s intellectual histories and African, Islamic, South Asian and Latin American traditions still need much fuller coverage.

strands.title: History of ideas and recurring concepts
strands.focus: Lovejoy follows changing combinations of ideas across philosophical, religious and literary materials.

strands.title: Arguments, languages and historical action
strands.focus: Skinner, Pocock and Brett pursue distinct contextual inquiries; they are not interchangeable statements of one method.

strands.title: Conceptual change and historical time
strands.focus: Koselleck relates semantic change to social history without making concepts and social structures identical.

strands.title: Texts, contexts and experience
strands.focus: LaCapra develops textual criticism; Toews’s titled intervention marks a related debate whose detailed claims remain a reading task.

strands.title: Publishing and the circulation of ideas
strands.focus: Darnton connects thought with the material and commercial work of producing and distributing books. Chartier’s later studies follow texts’ mobility across attributions, printed versions, genres and translations, in his reviewers’ accounts.

strands.title: Japanese political thought and translation
strands.focus: Maruyama’s Tokugawa studies and Hane’s translation widen the selection while leaving its modernization interpretation open to scrutiny.
strands.works: Studies in the Intellectual History of Tokugawa Japan (English 1974)
